edges.description: NMDA-receptor (GluN2A) dysfunction perturbs development of perisylvian speech-language networks and the hippocampus.
Altered NMDA-receptor (GluN2A) signaling produces a hyperexcitable cortical/subcortical substrate that gives rise to sleep-activated epileptiform activity.
Sleep-activated epileptiform activity in speech cortex drives the acquired language regression.
Sleep onset activates focal or multifocal epileptiform discharges into continuous or nearly continuous spike-and-wave activity during slow-wave sleep.
edges.target: Continuous Spike and Waves During Slow Sleep (ESES/CSWS)

edges.description: Cortical hyperexcitability manifests interictally as focal centrotemporal or posterotemporal spike-and-wave discharges on EEG.
edges.target: EEG with Centrotemporal Focal Spike Waves

edges.description: Hyperexcitable perisylvian and centrotemporal networks generate clinical seizures in 70% to 80% of patients.
Disruption of auditory-language cortex causes receptive failure to recognize spoken words ("word deafness") despite intact peripheral hearing.
Focal developmental regression of language skills after normal initial acquisition culminates in acquired receptive and expressive aphasia.
Epileptiform disruption of speech-language and cognitive networks drives language and/or global developmental regression.

Behavioral disturbances including irritability, hyperkinesis, attention-deficit disorder, and autistic behaviors frequently accompany the acquired aphasia and language regression in Landau-Kleffner syndrome.

nodes.description: Progressive loss of previously acquired language, with receptive language most affected, followed by deterioration of expressive language. This acquired epileptic aphasia is the defining feature of LKS.

evidence.reference_title: GRIN2A mutations in acquired epileptic aphasia and related childhood focal epilepsies and encephalopathies with speech and language dysfunction.
evidence.snippet: Acquired epileptic aphasia (Landau-Kleffner syndrome, LKS) and continuous spike and waves during slow-wave sleep syndrome (CSWSS) represent rare and closely related childhood focal epileptic encephalopathies of unknown etiology.

nodes.description: Impaired recognition/comprehension of spoken language ("word deafness") with a normal audiogram. The receptive deficit is often the earliest and most prominent feature and may initially be mistaken for deafness.

evidence.reference_title: Treatment of Epileptic Encephalopathies: Current State of the Art.
evidence.snippet: This aphasia takes the form of an auditory agnosia; in contrast to the language deficit in electrical status epilepticus in sleep, where there is a primarily expressive aphasia with intact comprehension, children with Landau-Kleffner syndrome may appear to be unconscious of spoken words, or effectively deaf.

nodes.description: Children frequently develop behavioral disturbances including hyperactivity, inattention, aggression, and autistic-like features, which often accompany the language regression.

evidence.reference_title: Update on the genetics of the epilepsy-aphasia spectrum and role of GRIN2A mutations.
evidence.snippet: epileptic encephalopathies with acquired cognitive, behavioral and speech and/or language impairment

nodes.description: High-dose benzodiazepines (e.g., diazepam, clobazam) are among the most frequently used first-line therapies for the sleep-activated epileptiform activity (ESES/CSWS) underlying LKS and the epilepsy-aphasia spectrum. In a multicenter cohort, benzodiazepines were associated with greater odds of clinical improvement than other antiseizure medications.

evidence.reference_title: Treatment Practices and Outcomes in Continuous Spike and Wave during Slow Wave Sleep: A Multicenter Collaboration.
evidence.snippet: Benzodiazepines and ASMs are the most frequent initial therapy prescribed for CSWS in the US. Our data suggests that ASMs are inferior to benzodiazepines and steroids and support earlier use of these therapies.

nodes.description: Continuous or near-continuous spike-and-wave discharges activated during slow-wave sleep, the electroencephalographic hallmark of LKS and the epilepsy-aphasia spectrum. Discharges are frequently focal/centrotemporal and markedly potentiated by sleep.
nodes.id: Continuous Spike and Waves During Slow Sleep (ESES/CSWS)

evidence.snippet: electroencephalogram (EEG) abnormalities, including continuous spike-and-wave discharges in sleep or very active centrotemporal discharges

evidence.reference_title: Update on the genetics of the epilepsy-aphasia spectrum and role of GRIN2A mutations.
evidence.snippet: the epileptic Encephalopathy related to Status Epilepticus during slow Sleep syndrome (ESES)

nodes.description: Corticosteroids (and ACTH) are widely used to suppress the sleep-activated epileptiform activity and promote language recovery in LKS, particularly when started early.

evidence.reference_title: Treatment of electrical status epilepticus in sleep: Clinical and EEG characteristics and response to 147 treatments in 47 patients.
evidence.snippet: Steroid treatment was most successful in improving cognitive performance.

evidence.reference_title: Corticosteroids in childhood epilepsies: A systematic review.
evidence.snippet: In (D)EE-SWAS (nine studies, 126 patients), 64% of patients showed an improvement either in the EEG or in their language/cognition following various steroid treatment regimes.

nodes.description: Beyond language, some children show broader developmental, global, or cognitive regression, contributing to the encephalopathic nature of the disorder.

evidence.snippet: focal epilepsy with language and/or global developmental regression

nodes.description: Focal spike-and-wave discharges in the centrotemporal (perisylvian) regions, overlapping electroclinically with rolandic epilepsy.
nodes.id: EEG with Centrotemporal Focal Spike Waves

evidence.snippet: continuous spike-and-wave discharges in sleep or very active centrotemporal discharges

nodes.description: In approximately 20% of LKS/epilepsy-aphasia spectrum cases, de novo or inherited pathogenic variants in GRIN2A alter the function of the GluN2A (NR2A) subunit of the NMDA glutamate receptor. Disrupted NMDA receptor signaling perturbs excitatory glutamatergic neurotransmission and synaptic plasticity in cortical neurons, providing the molecular substrate for the epileptic encephalopathy.

evidence.reference_title: GRIN2A mutations in acquired epileptic aphasia and related childhood focal epilepsies and encephalopathies with speech and language dysfunction.
evidence.snippet: about 20% of cases of LKS, CSWSS and electroclinically atypical rolandic epilepsy often associated with speech impairment can have a genetic origin sustained by de novo or inherited mutations in the GRIN2A gene (encoding the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) glutamate receptor α2 subunit, GluN2A)

evidence.reference_title: GRIN2A mutations cause epilepsy-aphasia spectrum disorders.
evidence.snippet: We report the first monogenic cause, to our knowledge, for EAS. GRIN2A mutations are restricted to this group of cases

nodes.description: In individuals with GRIN2A loss-of-function/null variants, treatment with the NMDAR coagonist L-serine has been associated with improvements in behavior, development, EEG, and/or seizure frequency. CAUTION: in gain-of-function (NMDAR-activating) missense variants, NMDAR agonists/ activators such as L-serine should be avoided as they may worsen symptoms.

evidence.snippet: treatment with the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) coagonist L-serine was associated with improvements in behavior, development, EEG features, and/or seizure frequency

In individuals with GRIN2A-related disorders due to pathogenic missense variants activating the NMDAR (i.e., gain-of-function variants), receptor-specific agonists and other activators (e.g., L-serine) should be avoided as this could result in worsening of symptoms.

nodes.description: Sleep-activated epileptiform disruption of perisylvian language cortex produces acquired loss of previously developed language, characteristically beginning with impaired auditory verbal comprehension (auditory verbal agnosia) and progressing to broader receptive and expressive language loss, sometimes with associated behavioral and cognitive regression.

evidence.reference_title: GRIN2A mutations cause epilepsy-aphasia spectrum disorders.
evidence.snippet: Epilepsy-aphasia syndromes (EAS) are a group of rare, severe epileptic encephalopathies of unknown etiology with a characteristic electroencephalogram (EEG) pattern and developmental regression particularly affecting language.

nodes.description: Structural MRI in individuals with pathogenic GRIN2A variants and epilepsy-aphasia syndromes shows altered development of classical speech-language networks: increased cortical thickness/volume in perisylvian regions (posterior Broca's area, superior temporal region) and reduced left hippocampal volume, indicating that NMDA-receptor dysfunction perturbs speech-language network development.

evidence.reference_title: Perisylvian and Hippocampal Anomalies in Individuals With Pathogenic GRIN2A Variants.
evidence.snippet: Anomalies in perisylvian regions, with largest differences in Broca's area, suggest an altered development of classical speech-language networks in GRIN2A-related EAS.

nodes.description: Most children with LKS have clinical epileptic seizures, which may be focal or generalized; seizures are often infrequent and can precede or follow the onset of language regression.

evidence.snippet: Epilepsy features include seizure onset usually between ages three and six years, focal epilepsy with language and/or global developmental regression

nodes.description: Pathological hyperexcitability produces marked activation of focal, typically perisylvian/centrotemporal, spike-and-wave discharges during non-REM (slow-wave) sleep, reaching continuous or near-continuous spike and waves during slow sleep (electrical status epilepticus in sleep, ESES/CSWS). This sleep-potentiated epileptiform activity in language cortex is thought to disrupt the maturation and function of language networks during a critical developmental window.

evidence.reference_title: Landau-Kleffner syndrome. Treatment with subpial intracortical transection.
evidence.snippet: It is thought to be the result of an epileptogenic lesion arising in speech cortex during a critical period of development.

evidence.reference_title: Update on the genetics of the epilepsy-aphasia spectrum and role of GRIN2A mutations.
evidence.snippet: RE is part of a single and continuous spectrum of childhood epilepsies and epileptic encephalopathies with acquired cognitive, behavioral and speech and/or language impairment, known as the epilepsy-aphasia spectrum (EAS)
